posts.author: dave battin
posts.content_md: I wanted to put together an LCD screen for doing multiplex holography, and i am wondering about the possibility of using one of the new types of LCD picture frames? All the pictures could be run thru photo editing then shown one at a time. I hate to blow $125 and then see it not work (on the other hand it wouldn’t be the first time I blew $125 on holography)! LOL

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
What are the details of the LCD screen? Is it monitor sized? Resolution? Dynamic Range? Front lit or back lit?

It seems to me from experience that contrast is probably the most important of these parameters.

And there is nothing wrong with projecting an image from a small LCD or DMD.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
This is going to be an exciting topic in the comming years. I am seeing LCD screens come down in price each week in the paper. I have a fairly cheap 42" LCD in my bedroom. 

The TI projection TV go down in price regularly and I am seeing LCD projectors on ebay for a few hundred dollars. It is only a matter of time before many holographers are using this technology. The basic version of it seems pretty simple.

Ed, are you fimiliar with the predistortion routines developed at MIT for making the images at the edges of a flat multiplex replay without distortion?

The Liti hologram I hae is very well done. I assume since they record in the round and store the hologram on a flat piece of film that there is a fair amount of compensation. I remember hearing that MIT had developed the process but I have not read any of the papers.

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md: I am not so sure of why they needed to pre-distort things. From my experience with stereograms we didn't attempt anything exotic and everything looked just dandy.

posts.author: favalora
posts.content_md:
Colin -

Mike Halle (Boston, MA) was the first author (along with Benton, a Zebra founder, etc.) on the predistortion work @ MIT. Sounds like you already have the link to his paper; his website links to his [The Ultragram](http://splweb.bwh.harvard.edu:8000/pages/ppl/halazar/) work.

g

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md:
I think it was Lloyd Huff that first described the "slice & dice" technique for making one-step stereograms. His paper is in the proceedings from the first International Symposium on Display Holography. 

Ken Haines patented a technique for using a curved master to make flat stereograms in the late '70s I think. His system may still be in use at ABNH.
